entries.5454c86638ec7dd8ded2674bacedcc36fb2c065d: <div sID="gen13099" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="136" osisID="Ps.136" sID="Ps.136"/> <div eID="gen13099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13100" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13101" type="x-p"/> The scope of this psalm is the same with that of the <reference osisRef="Ps.135.1-Ps.135.21">foregoing psalm</reference>, but there is something very singular in the composition of it; for the latter half of each verse is the same, repeated throughout the psalm, "for his mercy endureth for ever," and yet no vain repetition. It is allowed that such burdens, or "keepings," as we call them, add very much to the beauty of a song, and help to make it moving and affecting; nor can any verse contain more weighty matter, or more worthy to be thus repeated, than this, that God's mercy endureth for ever; and the repetition of it here twenty-six times intimates, 1. That God's mercies to his people are thus repeated and drawn, as it were, with a continuando from the beginning to the end, with a progress and advance in infinitum. 2. That in every particular favour we ought to take notice of the mercy of God, and to take favour we ought to take notice of the mercy of God, and to take notice of it as enduring still, the same now that it has been, and enduring for ever, the same always that it is. 3. That the everlasting continuance of the mercy of God is very much his honour and that which he glories in, and very much the saints' comfort and that which they glory in. It is that which therefore our hearts should be full of and greatly affected with, so that the most frequent mention of it, instead of cloying us, should raise us the more, because it will be the subject of our praise to all eternity. This most excellent sentence, that God's mercy endureth for ever, is magnified above all the truths concerning God, not only by the repetition of it here, but by the signal tokens of divine acceptance with which God owned the singing of it, both in Solomon's time (<reference osisRef="2Chr.5.13">2 Chron. v. 13</reference>, when they sang these words, "for his mercy endureth for ever," the house was filled with a cloud) and in Jehoshaphat's time (when they sang these words, God gave them victory, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21-2Chr.20.22">2 Chron. xx. 21, 22</reference>), which should make us love to sing, "His mercies sure do still endure, eternally." We must praise God, I. As great and good in himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.1-Ps.136.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. As the Creator of the world, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.5-Ps.136.9">ver. 5-9</reference>. III. As Israel's God and Saviour, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.10-Ps.136.22">ver. 10-22</reference>. IV. As our Redeemer, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.23-Ps.136.24">ver. 23, 24</reference>. V. As the great benefactor of the whole creation, and God over all, blessed for evermore, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.25-Ps.136.26">ver. 25, 26</reference>.
entries.66d6c6e2dedc305e15acb59eb71cc368799579b7: <div eID="gen13101" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13100" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortations to Thanksgiving.</title> <div sID="gen13102" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O give thanks unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for <hi type="italic">he is</hi> good: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">2</hi> O give thanks unto the God of gods: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">3</hi> O give thanks to the Lord of lords: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">4</hi> To him who alone doeth great wonders: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">5</hi> To him that by wisdom made the heavens: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">6</hi> To him that stretched out the earth above the waters: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">7</hi> To him that made great lights: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">8</hi> The sun to rule by day: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">9</hi> The moon and stars to rule by night: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <div eID="gen13102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13103" type="x-p"/> The duty we are here again and again called to is to <hi type="italic">give thanks,</hi> to <hi type="italic">offer the sacrifice of praise continually,</hi> not the fruits of our ground or cattle, but <hi type="italic">the fruit of our lips, giving thanks to his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>. We are never so earnestly called upon to pray and repent as to <hi type="italic">give thanks;</hi> for it is the will of God that we should abound most in the most pleasant exercises of religion, in that which is the work of heaven. Now here observe, 1. Whom we must give thanks to—to him that we receive all good from, <hi type="italic">to the Lord,</hi> Jehovah, Israel's God (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">the God of gods,</hi> the God whom angels adore, from whom magistrates derive their power, and by whom all pretended deities are and shall be conquered (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">to the Lord of lords,</hi> the Sovereign of all sovereigns, the stay and supporter of all supports; <reference osisRef="Ps.136.3">v. 3</reference>. In all our adorations we must have an eye to God's excellency as transcendent, and to his power and dominion as incontestably and uncontrollably supreme. 2. What we must give thanks for, not as the Pharisee that made all his thanksgivings terminate in his own praise (<hi type="italic">God, I thank thee,</hi> that I am so and so), but directing them all to God's glory. (1.) We must give thanks to God for his goodness and mercy (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give thanks to the Lord,</hi> not only because he does good, but because he is good (all the streams must be traced up to the fountain), not only because he is merciful to us, but because his mercy endures for ever, and will be drawn out to those that shall come after us. We must give thanks to God, not only for that mercy which is now handed out to us here on earth, but for that which shall endure for ever in the glories and joys of heaven. (2.) We must give God thanks for the instances of his power and wisdom. In general (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.4">v. 4</reference>), he <hi type="italic">alone does great wonders.</hi> The contrivance is wonderful, the design being laid by infinite wisdom; the performance is wonderful, being put in execution by infinite power. He alone does marvellous things; none besides can do such things, and he does them without the assistance or advice of any other. More particularly, [1.] He made the heavens, and stretched them out, and in them we not only see his wisdom and power, but we taste his mercy in their benign influences; as long as the heavens endure the mercy of God endures in them, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.5">v. 5</reference>. [2.] He raised the earth out of the waters when he caused the dry land to appear, that it might be fit to be a habitation for man, and therein also his mercy to man still endures (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.6">v. 6</reference>); for <hi type="italic">the earth hath he given to the children of men,</hi> and all its products. [3.] Having made both heaven and earth, he settled a correspondence between them, notwithstanding their distance, by making the sun, moon, and stars, which he placed in the firmament of heaven, to shed their light and influences upon this earth, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.7-Ps.136.9">v. 7-9</reference>. These are called the <hi type="italic">great lights</hi> because they appear so to us, for otherwise astronomers could tell us that the moon is less than many of the stars, but, being nearer to the earth, it seems much greater. They are said to <hi type="italic">rule,</hi> not only because they govern the seasons of the year, but because they are useful to the world, and benefactors are the best rulers, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.25">Luke xxii. 25</reference>. But the empire is divided, one <hi type="italic">rules by day,</hi> the <hi type="italic">other by night</hi> (at least, <hi type="italic">the stars</hi>), and yet all are subject to God's direction and disposal. Those rulers, therefore, which the Gentiles idolized, are the world's servants and God's subjects. <hi type="italic">Sun, stand thou still, and thou moon.</hi>
entries.606c28680d73cef894187c583f7d7a31f0f6815f: <div eID="gen13103" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Divine Mercy Celebrated.</title> <div sID="gen13104" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> To him that smote Egypt in their firstborn: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">11</hi> And brought out Israel from among them: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: 12 With a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">13</hi> To him which divided the Red sea into parts: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">14</hi> And made Israel to pass through the midst of it: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">15</hi> But overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red sea: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">16</hi> To him which led his people through the wilderness: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">17</hi> To him which smote great kings: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">18</hi> And slew famous kings: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">19</hi> Sihon king of the Amorites: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: 20 And Og the king of Bashan: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">21</hi> And gave their land for a heritage: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">22</hi> <hi type="italic">Even</hi> a heritage unto Israel his servant: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <div eID="gen13104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13105" type="x-p"/> The great things God for Israel, when he first formed them into a people, and set up his kingdom among them, are here mentioned, as often elsewhere in the psalms, as instances both of the power of God and of the particular kindness he had for Israel. See <reference osisRef="Ps.135.8">Ps. cxxxv. 8</reference>, &c. 1. He brought them out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.10-Ps.136.12">v. 10-12</reference>. That was a mercy which endured long to them, and our redemption by Christ, which was typified by that, does indeed endure for ever, for it is an eternal redemption. Of all the plagues of Egypt, none is mentioned but the death of the first-born, because that was the conquering plague; by that God, who in all the plagues distinguished the Israelites from the Egyptians, brought them at last from among them, not by a wile, but with a strong hand and an arm stretched out to reach far and do great things. These miracles of mercy, as they proved Moses's commission to give law to Israel, so they laid Israel under lasting obligations to obey that law, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.2">Exod. xx. 2</reference>. 2. He forced them a way through the Red Sea, which obstructed them at their first setting out. By the power he has to control the common course of nature he <hi type="italic">divided the sea into two parts,</hi> between which he opened a path, and made Israel to pass between the parts, now that they were to enter into covenant with him; see <reference osisRef="Jer.34.18">Jer. xxxiv. 18</reference>. He not only divided the sea, but gave his people courage to go through it when it was divided, which was an instance of God's power over men's hearts, as the former of his power over the waters. And, to make it a miracle of justice as well as mercy, the same Red Sea that was a lane to the Israelites was a grave to their pursuers. There he shook off Pharaoh and his host. 3. He conducted them through a vast howling wilderness (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.16">v. 16</reference>); there he led them and fed them. Their camp was victualled and fortified by a constant series of miracles for forty years; though they loitered and wandered there, they were not lost. And in this the mercy of God, and the constancy of that mercy, were the more observable because they often provoked him in the wilderness and grieved him in the desert. 4. He destroyed kings before them, to make room for them (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.17-Ps.136.18">v. 17, 18</reference>), not deposed and banished them, but smote and slew them, in which appeared his wrath against them, but his mercy, his never-failing mercy, to Israel. And that which magnified it was that they were <hi type="italic">great kings</hi> and <hi type="italic">famous kings,</hi> yet God subdued them as easily as if they had been the least, and weakest, and meanest, of the children of men. They were wicked kings, and then their grandeur and lustre would not secure them from the justice of God. The more great and famous they were the more did God's mercy to Israel appear in giving such kings for them. Sihon and Og are particularly mentioned, because they were the first two that were conquered on the other side Jordan, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.19-Ps.136.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. It is good to enter into the detail of God's favours and not to view them in the gross, and in each instance to observe, and own, that God's <hi type="italic">mercy endureth for ever.</hi> 5. He put them in possession of a good land, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.21-Ps.136.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. He whose the earth is, and the fulness thereof, the world and those that dwell therein, took land from one people and gave it to another, as pleased him. The <hi type="italic">iniquity of the Amorites was now full,</hi> and therefore it was taken from them. <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> was his <hi type="italic">servant,</hi> and, though they had been provoking in the wilderness, yet he intended to have some service out of them, for <hi type="italic">to them pertained the service of God.</hi> As he said to the Egyptians, <hi type="italic">Let my people go,</hi> so to the Canaanites, <hi type="italic">Let my people in,</hi> that they may serve me. In this <hi type="italic">God's mercy</hi> to them <hi type="italic">endureth for ever,</hi> because it was a figure of the heavenly Canaan, the <hi type="italic">mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.</hi>
entries.576a9f10beaab5c1867eaac14d8c2f50e375380b: <div eID="gen13105" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Divine Mercy Celebrated.</title> <div sID="gen13106" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Who remembered us in our low estate: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="super">24</hi> And hath redeemed us from our enemies: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">25</hi> Who giveth food to all flesh: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. 26 O give thanks unto the God of heaven: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <div eID="gen13106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13107" type="x-p"/> God's everlasting mercy is here celebrated, 1. In the redemption of his church, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.23-Ps.136.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. In the many redemptions wrought for the Jewish church out of the hands of their oppressors (when, in the years of their servitude, their estate was very low, God remembered them, and raised them up saviours, the judges, and David, at length, by whom God gave them rest from all their enemies), but especially in the great redemption of the universal church, of which these were types, we have a great deal of reason to say, "<hi type="italic">He remembered us,</hi> the children of men, <hi type="italic">in our low estate,</hi> in our lost estate, <hi type="italic">for his mercy endureth for ever;</hi> he sent his Son to redeem us from sin, and death, and hell, and all our spiritual enemies, <hi type="italic">for his mercy endureth for ever;</hi> he was sent to redeem us, and not the angels that sinned, for his mercy endureth for ever." 2. In the provision he makes for all the creatures (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">He gives food to all flesh.</hi> It is an instance of the mercy of God's providence that wherever he has given life he gives food agreeable and sufficient; and he is a good housekeeper that provides for so large a family. 3. In all his glories, and all his gifts (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give thanks to the God of heaven.</hi> This denotes him to be a glorious God, and the glory of his mercy is to be taken notice of in our praises. The <hi type="italic">riches of his glory</hi> are displayed in the <hi type="italic">vessels of his mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.9.23">Rom. ix. 23</reference>. It also denotes him to be the great benefactor, <hi type="italic">for every good and perfect gift is from above,</hi> from the Father of lights, the <hi type="italic">God of heaven;</hi> and we should trace every stream to the fountain. This and that particular mercy may perhaps endure but a while, but the mercy that is in God <hi type="italic">endures for ever;</hi> it is an inexhaustible fountain.  <chapter eID="Ps.136"/> <div eID="gen13107" type="x-p"/>

entries.a913146536c4674217833191c683db90324624a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7063"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 136</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.1-Ps.136.26">Psa 136:1-26</reference>. The theme is the same as that of Psalm 135. God should be praised for His works of creation and providence, His deliverance and care of His people, and judgments on their enemies, and His goodness to all. The chorus to every verse is in terms of that of <reference osisRef="Ps.106.1">Psa 106:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.1-Ps.118.4">118:1-4</reference>, and was perhaps used as the Amen by the people, in worship (compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.45">Psa 105:45</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen10834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7063"/>1-3. The divine titles denote supremacy. <div eID="gen10834" type="x-p"/>

entries.d8f087a42b8f0be972c0bf18cb85ab3f1b532f14: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7065"/><div sID="gen10836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7065"/><hi type="bold">5-6. by wisdom--</hi>or, "in wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.24">Psa 104:24</reference>).<div eID="gen10836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made--</hi>literally, "maker of."<div eID="gen10837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">above the waters--</hi>or, "higher than the waters" (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.2">Psa 24:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10838" type="x-p"/>

entries.b70624e1efb999530559e00bd5dfef7e4715094b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7067"/><div sID="gen10840" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7067"/><hi type="bold">15. overthrew--</hi>literally, "shook off," as in <reference osisRef="Exod.14.27">Ex 14:27</reference>, as a contemptuous rejection of a reptile. <div eID="gen10840" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b93066476a07fe60dd18059b221062921d01c57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7068"/><div sID="gen10841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7068"/><hi type="bold">23. remembered us--</hi>or, "for us" (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.1">Psa 132:1</reference>).<div eID="gen10841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our low estate--</hi>that is, captivity. <div eID="gen10842" type="x-p"/>
entries.d269ef488e11f2293e938c04e4f286b30881d05f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7069"/><div sID="gen10843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7069"/><hi type="bold">24. entries.1e98715db6b517082fd5a4297124631a8ff03016: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7070"/><div sID="gen10844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7070"/>25. entries.f8a1d6c3fab712e8fc7a9146e3a0017d00526b37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7071"/><div sID="gen10845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7071"/><hi type="bold">26. entries.83dc23ed3b88cb7e116e1949e1db04d2b4ff0ed1: <div eID="gen23248" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23249" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23250" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23250" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23249" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23251" type="x-p"/> An exhortation to give thanks to God for various mercies granted to all men, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.1-Psa.136.9">Psa 136:1-9</reference>; particularly to the Israelites in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.10-Psa.136.12">Psa 136:10-12</reference>; at the Red Sea, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.13-Psa.136.15">Psa 136:13-15</reference>; in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.16-Psa.136.20">Psa 136:16-20</reference>; and in the promised land, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.21">Psa 136:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.22">Psa 136:22</reference>; for the redemption of the captives from Babylon <reference osisRef="Psa.136.23">Psa 136:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.24">Psa 136:24</reference>; and for his providential mercies to all, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.25">Psa 136:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.136.26">Psa 136:26</reference>. <div eID="gen23251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23252" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is little else than a repetition of the preceding, with the burden, כי לעולם חסדו ki leolam chasdo, "because his mercy endureth for ever," at the end of every verse. See below. It seems to have been a responsive song: the first part of the verse sung by the Levites, the burden by the people. It has no title in the Hebrew, nor in any of the Versions. It was doubtless written after the captivity. The author is unknown. <div eID="gen23252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23253" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23254" type="x-p"/> O give thanks unto the Lord: for he is good - This sentiment often occurs: the goodness of the Divine nature, both as a ground of confidence and of thanksgiving. <div eID="gen23254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23255" type="x-p"/> For his mercy endureth for ever - These words, which are the burden of every verse, כי לעולם חסדו ki leolam chasdo, might be translated: "For his tender mercy is to the coming age:" meaning, probably, if the Psalm be prophetic, that peculiar display of his compassion, the redemption of the world by the Lord Jesus. These very words were prescribed by David as an acknowledgment, to be used continually in the Divine worship, see <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.41">1Chr 16:41</reference> : also by Solomon, <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.3">2Chr 7:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.6">2Chr 7:6</reference>, and observed by Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2Chr 20:21</reference>; all acknowledging that, however rich in mercy God was to them, the most extensive displays of his goodness were reserved for the age to come; see <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10-1Pet.1.12">1Pet 1:10-12</reference> : "Of which salvation the prophets have inquired, and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that should come unto you, - unto whom it was revealed, that not unto themselves, but unto us, they did minister the things which are now reported unto you by them that preached the Gospel unto you by the power of the Holy Ghost sent down from heaven," etc.
entries.5d425c485a169c1593c125109735df4ab5d62b06: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23256" type="x-p"/> The God of gods - לאדני האדנים ladonai haadonim. As adonai signifies director, etc., it may apply here, not to idols, for God is not their god; but to the priests and spiritual rulers; as Lord of lords may apply to kings and magistrates, etc. He is God and ruler over all the rulers of the earth, whether in things sacred or civil.
entries.7a9eed1c4e66ddd72f1eb704cde84d1251e6d2b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23257" type="x-p"/> Who alone doeth great wonders - Miracles. No power but that which is almighty can work miracles, נפלאות niphlaoth, the inversion, or suspension, or destruction of the laws of nature.
entries.09bdd0e8578e5736e3cc94d4381c8a6b16633d01: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23258" type="x-p"/> By wisdom made the heavens - In the contrivance of the celestial bodies, in their relations, connexions, influences on each other, revolutions, etc., the wisdom of God particularly appears.
entries.38cb379bfc6a089923216cdf214ec760b1c41e95: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23259" type="x-p"/> Stretched out the earth above the waters - Or, upon the waters. This seems to refer to a central abyss of waters, the existence of which has not been yet disproved.
entries.23c71f324e7caf64d78e75d9583b93f372ca0c83: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23260" type="x-p"/> Great lights - See the notes on the parallel passages in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.1">Gen 1:1</reference>, etc.
entries.ac1a10fc192ca476e7549245293d5c6ceb0aed28: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23261" type="x-p"/> Smote Egypt in their first-born - This was one of the heaviest of strokes: a great part of the rising generation was cut off; few but old persons and children left remaining.
entries.6edafc607bebc8ae7db4e88c845f13b6efb8fbcc: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23262" type="x-p"/> Divided the Red Sea into parts - Some of the Jews have imagined that God made twelve paths through the Red Sea, that each tribe might have a distinct passage. Many of the fathers were of the same opinion; but is this very likely?
entries.6510c66cf2f570277c46008650a1f6f2efc11401: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23263" type="x-p"/> Which led his people through the wilderness - It was an astonishing miracle of God to support so many hundreds of thousands of people in a wilderness totally deprived of all necessaries for the life of man, and that for the space of forty years.
entries.d631c78fd7da27445c9f10dcfe811b4e37a3dd7f: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen23263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23264" type="x-p"/> Who remembered us in our low estate - He has done much for our forefathers; and he has done much for us, in delivering us, when we had no helper, from our long captivity in Babylon.
entries.924641cb41d33531c113555fc7caed4112957565: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen23264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23265" type="x-p"/> Giveth food to all flesh - By whose universal providence every intellectual and animal being is supported and preserved. The appointing every living thing food, and that sort of food which is suited to its nature, (and the nature and habits of animals are endlessly diversified), is an overwhelming proof of the wondrous providence, wisdom, and goodness of God. <div eID="gen23265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23266" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon, add a twenty-seventh verse, by repeating here <reference osisRef="Psa.136.3">Psa 136:3</reference> very unnecessarily.  <chapter eID="Ps.136"/> <div eID="gen23266" type="x-p"/>

entries.cc5cddfb71aa191101015a72332db24c431b822e: <div eID="gen10253" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">O Give Thanks unto the Lord, for He Is Good</title> <div sID="gen10254" type="x-p"/> The cry <reference osisRef="Ps.135.3">Psa 135:3</reference>, <hi type="italic">Praise ye Jāh , for good is Jahve</hi>, is here followed by a <hi type="italic">Hodu</hi>, the last of the collection, with “for His goodness endureth for ever” repeated twenty-six times as a <hi type="italic">versus intercalaris</hi>. In the liturgical language this Psalm is called <hi type="italic">par excellence</hi> the great Hallel, for according to its broadest compass the great Hallel comprehends Ps 120-136,<,<note placement="foot">There are three opinions in the Talmud and Midrash concerning the compass of the “Great Hallel,” viz., (1) <reference osisRef="Ps.136.2">Ps 136, (2</reference>) Ps. 135:4-136:26, (3) Ps 120-136.</note> whilst the Hallel which is absolutely so called extends from <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference> to Ps 118. Down to <reference osisRef="Ps.136.18">Psa 136:18</reference> the song and counter-song organize themselves into hexastichic groups or strophes, which, however, from <reference osisRef="Ps.136.19">Psa 136:19</reference> (and therefore from the point where the dependence on Ps 135, already begun with <reference osisRef="Ps.136.17">Psa 136:17</reference>, becomes a borrowing, onwards) pass over into octastichs. In Heidenheim’s Psalter the Psalm appears (after Norzi) in two columns (like Deut. 32), which it is true has neither tradition (vid., Ps 18) nor MSS precedent in its favour, but really corresponds to its structure.
entries.6f58c8ea71fd3b2fe61c29a51d99c94d18983df0: <reference osisRef="Ps.136.1-Ps.136.9">Psa 136:1-9</reference> <div eID="gen10254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10255" type="x-p"/> Like the preceding Psalm, this Psalm allies itself to the Book of Deuteronomy. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.2">Psa 136:2</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.3">Psa 136:3</reference></hi> (<hi type="italic">God of gods and Lord of lords</hi>) are taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.10.17">Deu 10:17</reference>; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.12">Psa 136:12</reference></hi> (<hi type="italic">with a strong hand and stretched-out arm</hi>) from <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deu 4:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.15">Deu 5:15</reference>, and frequently (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.32.21">Jer 32:21</reference>); <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.16">Psa 136:16</reference></hi> like <reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jer 2:6</reference>). With reference to the Deuteronomic colouring of <reference osisRef="Ps.136.19-Ps.136.22">Psa 136:19-22</reference>, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.135.10-Ps.135.12">Psa 135:10-12</reference>; also the expression “Israel His servant” recalls <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deu 32:36</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.135.14">Psa 135:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.13">Psa 90:13</reference>), and still more <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference>, where the comprehension of Israel under the unity of this notion has its own proper place. In other respects, too, the Psalm is an echo of earlier model passages. <hi type="italic">Who alone doeth great wonders</hi> sounds like <reference osisRef="Ps.72.18">Psa 72:18</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.10">Psa 86:10</reference>); and the adjective “great” that is added to “wonders” shows that the poet found the formula already in existence. In connection with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.5">Psa 136:5</reference></hi> he has <reference osisRef="Prov.3.19">Pro 3:19</reference> or <reference osisRef="Jer.10.12">Jer 10:12</reference> in his mind; תּבוּנה, like חכמה, is the demiurgic wisdom. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.6">Psa 136:6</reference></hi> calls to mind <reference osisRef="Isa.42.5">Isa 42:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">Isa 44:24</reference>; the expression is “above the waters,” as in <reference osisRef="Ps.34.2">Psa 34:2</reference> “upon the seas,” because the water is partly visible and partly invisible מתּחת לארץ (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.4">Exo 20:4</reference>). The plural אורים, <hi type="italic">luces</hi>, instead of מארות, <hi type="italic">lumina</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.8">Eze 32:8</reference>, מאורי אור), is without precedent. It is a controverted point whether אורת in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa 26:19</reference> signifies lights (cf. אורה, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.12">Psa 139:12</reference>) or herbs (2Ki 4:39). The plural ממשׁלות is also rare (occurring only besides in <reference osisRef="Ps.114.2">Psa 114:2</reference>): it here denotes the dominion of the moon on the one hand, and (going beyond <reference osisRef="Gen.1.16">Gen 1:16</reference>) of the stars on the other. בּלּילה, like בּיּום, is the second member of the <hi type="italic">stat. construct.</hi>
entries.a0c355b3fdb2f0452a4f86c5dcc78eee379d0056: <reference osisRef="Ps.136.10-Ps.136.26">Psa 136:10-26</reference> <div eID="gen10255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10256" type="x-p"/> Up to this point it is God the absolute in general, the Creator of all things, to the celebration of whose praise they are summoned; and from this point onwards the God of the history of salvation. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.13">Psa 136:13</reference></hi> גּזר (instead of בּקע, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.13">Psa 78:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.14.21">Exo 14:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.11">Neh 9:11</reference>) of the dividing of the Red Sea is peculiar; גּזרים (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Gen 15:17</reference>, side by side with בּתרים) are the pieces or parts of a thing that is cut up into pieces. נער is a favourite word taken from Exo 14:27. With reference to the name of the Egyptian ruler <hi type="italic">Pharaoh</hi> (Herodotus also, ii. 111, calls the Pharaoh of the Exodus the son of Sesostris-Rameses Miumun, not Μενόφθας, as he is properly called, but absolutely Φερῶν), vid., on Psa 73:22. After the God to whom the praise is to be ascribed has been introduced with ל by always fresh attributes, the ל before the names of Sihon and of Og is perplexing. The words are taken over, as are the six lines of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.17-Ps.136.22">Psa 136:17-22</reference></hi> in the main, from <reference osisRef="Ps.135.10-Ps.135.12">Psa 135:10-12</reference>, with only a slight alteration in the expression. In <reference osisRef="Ps.136.23">Psa 136:23</reference> the continued influence of the construction הודוּ ל is at an end. The connection by means of שׁ (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.135.8">Psa 135:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.10">Psa 135:10</reference>) therefore has reference to the preceding “for His goodness endureth for ever.” The language here has the stamp of the latest period. It is true זכר with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> of the object is used even in the earliest Hebrew, but שׁפל is only authenticated by <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">Ecc 10:6</reference>, and פּרק, to break loose = to rescue (the customary Aramaic word for redemption), by <reference osisRef="Lam.5.8">Lam 5:8</reference>, just as in the closing verse, which recurs to the beginning, “God of heaven” is a name for God belonging to the latest literature, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.4">Neh 1:4</reference>; Neh 2:4. In <reference osisRef="Ps.136.23">Psa 136:23</reference> the praise changes suddenly to that which has been experienced very recently. The attribute in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.136.25">Psa 136:25</reference></hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.147.9">Psa 147:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.15">Psa 145:15</reference>) leads one to look back to a time in which famine befell them together with slavery.  <chapter eID="Ps.136"/> <div eID="gen10256" type="x-p"/>

entries.fedb5d0cb0a11f2ced028f0a152b93849c3b741d:
PSALM 136
The Psalmist reminds the Lord’s people, that unless they were assiduous in his praises, they were chargeable with defrauding him of what was justly due to him for his benefits. And, in mentioning each benefit, he takes particular notice of the mercy of God, to teach us how necessary it is to the proper celebration of his praises that we own everything which we receive from him to be bestowed gratuitously.
This Psalm is called by the Jews, the Great Thanksgiving.
Psalm 136:1-9
1. Praise Jehovah, for he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever. 2. Praise the Cod of gods, for his mercy endureth for ever. 3.. Praise the Lord of Lords,
“The three first verses of this Psalm contain the three several names of the Deity, which are commonly rendered Jehovah, God, and Lord, respectively; the first having reference to his essence as self-existent, and being his proper name; the second designating him under the character of a Judge or of an all-powerful being, if Aleim be derived from Al; and the third, Adoni, representing him as exercising rule.” — Cresswell.
for his mercy endureth for ever. 4. Who alone hath done great wonders, for his mercy endureth for ever, 5. Who made the heavens by his wisdom, [or, intelligently,] for his mercy endureth for ever. 6. Who stretcheth out the earth above the waters, for his mercy endureth for ever. 7. Who made the great lights, for his mercy endureth for ever. 8. The sun for rule by day, for his mercy endureth for ever. 9. The moon and stars for rule by night for his mercy endureth for ever.
 
1. For his mercy,
Jebb observes, that “the 136th Psalm is altogether peculiar in its construction, as it has the recurrence of the same words, ‘For everlasting is his mercy,’ at the end of every distich.” He adds, that “this elaborate artifice of construction seems characteristic of that later period which comprised the captivity and restoration;” although he at the same time admits, that it is to be found in Psalms of an earlier date than the Baby-lonish captivity, quoting a passage in the account of the dedication of Solomon’s Temple, which informs us, that the whole choir of Israel united in praising God “for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever:” and observing that this expression forms the.commencement of three other Psalms, the Psalm 106, Psalm 107, and Psalm 118. In his remarks on the Psalm 119, after adverting to the alphabetical character of that Psalm, he adds, “There are other artifices of construction observable in the Psalms and Hymns composed in these later ages of the Church. For example, that repetition of the same words and clauses, and the frequent recurrence of a characteristic word, so frequent in the Greater Hallel, [from the Psalm 111 to Psalm 118th, inclusive,] and in the Songs of Degrees: and in a continually recurring burden, in each distich, as in the Song of the three Children, and Psalm 136, which latter is unique in the Psalter. It has been the tendency of the poetry of most countries, in the progress of time, to make its characteristic features depend less upon the exactness of sentimental arrangement, and more upon some external artifice, whether this be prosodial metre, alliteration, rhyme, assonance, or the recurrence of a burthen. Now, though the poetry of the Scriptures, because it was inspired, never declined from the perfection of its sentimental construction, still those artificial contrivances, practiced, indeed, in earlier times, seem to have been more prevalent at the time of the captivity, and the time immediately following, than heretofore. It was probably so ordained, for the purpose of assisting the memories of the Jews, who at Babylon were excluded from the open exercise of their religion, and from public teaching, and, therefore, required more private helps, which could be more easily communicated orally from parents to children, or from masters to disciples.” — Jebb’s Translation of the Psalms, etc., volume 2.
etc. The insertion of this clause again and again in so many short and abrupt sentences, may seem a vain repetition, but verses repeated by way of chorus are both allowed and admired in profane poets, and why should we object to the reiteration in this instance, for which the best reasons can be shown, Men may not deny the divine goodness to be the source and Fountain of all their blessings, but the graciousness of his bounty is far from being fully and sincerely recognised, though the greatest stress is laid upon it in Scripture. Paul in speaking of it, (Romans 3:23,) calls it emphatically by the general term of the glory of God, intimating, that while God should be praised for all his works, it is his mercy principally that we should glorify. It is evident from what we read in sacred history, that it was customary for the Levites. according to the regulation laid down by David for conducting the praises of God, to sing by response, “for his mercy endureth for ever.” The practice was followed by Solomon in the dedication of the Temple, (2 Chronicles 7:3, 6,) and by Jehoshaphat in that solemn triumphal song mentioned in 2 Chronicles 20:21, of the same book. [Before proceeding to recite God’s works, the Psalmist declares his supreme Deity, and dominion, not that such comparative language implies that there is anything approaching] Deity besides him, but there is a disposition in men, whenever they see any part of his glory displayed, to conceive of a God separate from him, thus impiously dividing the Godhead into parts, and even proceeding so far as to frame gods of wood and stone. There is a depraved tendency in all to take delight in a multiplicity of gods. For this reason, apparently, the. Psalmist uses the plural number, not only in the word אלהים, Elohim, but in the word אדונים, Adonim, so that it reads literally, praise ye the Lords of Lords: he would intimate, that the fullest perfection of all dominion is to be found in the one God.

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXXVI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The matter of this Psalm is the same with the former, onely it is a little more fitted to the use and service of the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, by the continued repetition of that solemn clause, <ns0:hi>for thy mercy endures for ever,</ns0:hi> which was much used by the sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cred Singers. See 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 7. 3. & 20. 21.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 O <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 106. 1. & 107. 1. & 118. 1.</ns0:note> Give thanks unto the LORD, for <ns0:hi>he is</ns0:hi> good: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chr. 16. 41.</ns0:note> for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 O give thanks unto <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 10. 17.</ns0:note> the God of gods <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Who is infinitely superiour to all that are called <ns0:hi>gods,</ns0:hi> whether Angels, or Princes, or Idols.</ns0:note>: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 O give thanks unto the Lord of lords: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 To him who alone <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He and none else. Or, he without the help of any other person or thing, whereas no other being can do any thing alone or without his help.</ns0:note> doth great wonders: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 1. 1.</ns0:note> To him that by wisdom <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To wit, by eminent and admirable wisdom, far exceed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the capacity of all humane or Angelical creatures.</ns0:note> made the hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vens: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 1. 9. Je<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 10. 12.</ns0:note> To him that stretched out the earth a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove the waters <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Of which see on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1. 9. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 24. 2.</ns0:note>: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 1. 14.</ns0:note> To him that made great lights: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 The sun <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>lings by day.</ns0:note> to rule by day <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Of which phrase and the like in the next verse, see my Notes on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1. 16.</ns0:note>: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 The moon and stars to rule by night: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 12. 2.</ns0:note> To him that smote Egypt in their first<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />born: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 12. 51. & 13. 17.</ns0:note> And brought out Israel from among them: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 6. 6.</ns0:note> With a strong hand, and with a stretch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed out arm: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 14. 21, 22. Psal. 74. 13. & 78. 13</ns0:note> To him which divided the Red sea into parts: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And made Israel to pass through the midst of it <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To wit, without fear or danger, by comparing this with the next verse.</ns0:note>: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 14. 28.</ns0:note> But <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 15. 22.</ns0:note> To him which led his people through the wilderness <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Through that vast howling wilderness where there was neither way nor provision; through which none but the Al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mighty God could have safely conducted them.</ns0:note>: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 135. 10, 11.</ns0:note> To him which smote great kings: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 29. 7. Ps. 135. 10, 11.</ns0:note> And slew mighty kings: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 21. 23.</ns0:note> Sihon king of the Amorite: for his mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 12. 17.</ns0:note> And gave their land for an heritage: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>

Thus God calleth them all <ns0:hi>his first-born, Exod.</ns0:hi> 4. 22.</ns0:note>: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Who remembred us in our low estate: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And hath redeemed us from our enemies: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 104. 27. & 147. 9.</ns0:note> Who giveth food to all flesh <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either to all mankind: or to all living creatures. For which God deserves great praises, which the Psalmist by his example teacheth us to render to God for them, because those who are most concerned either cannot or do not per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />form this duty.</ns0:note>: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 O give thanks unto the God of heaven: for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever.</ns0:p>
